item.title: Collection of genomic and transcriptomic resources for Rhodnius kissing bugs, vectors of Chagas disease
item.description:
Marie Merle, Florence Mougel, Christophe Klopp, Gabin Rignault, Claire Capdevielle Dulac, Elaine Folly-Ramos, Carlos Eduardo Almeida, Jonathan Filée, et al.
Scientific Data
DOI: 10.1038/s41597-026-08888-4
Abstract Triatomine bugs (“kissing bugs”) are vectors of Trypanosoma cruzi , the causative agent of Chagas disease, a neglected tropical disease affecting millions of people in Latin America. We present genomic and transcriptomic datasets for thirteen species of the genus Rhodnius , an epidemiologically important lineage within Triatominae, encompassing both domiciliary and sylvatic taxa. Hybrid de novo genome assemblies were generated by combining Illumina short reads with PacBio or Oxford Nanopore long reads. Three assemblies were further scaffolded to chromosome scale using Hi-C data, confirming a conserved diploid organization comprising ten pairs of autosomes that display a high level of chromosomal synteny across species. Two sex chromosomes were also identified including Y chromosome sequences that had not previously been assembled in this group. Whole genome assembly sizes range from 269.8 to 676.1 Mb. Structural gene annotations were produced using RNA-seq prediction and repetitive elements were identified using de novo repeat modeling. Nuclear single-copy ortholog datasets were also compiled as reusable resources for phylogenomic applications and assembly consistency assessment. Predicted protein-coding gene counts range from 17,884 to 28,088 genes per assembly. Repetitive sequences comprise 25–38% of genome assemblies, with transposable elements representing 8–20%. Genome assembly gene-space completeness assessed using BUSCO reaches up to 95.1% of conserved insect orthologs. These datasets expand genomic representation within Triatominae and provide standardized multi-omic resources for comparative genomics, genome structure analyses, and vector biology research.

item.title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the Toco Toucan Ramphastos toco (Aves, Ramphastidae)
item.description:
Guilherme Mota-Souza, Luohao Xu, Rafael Kretschmer, Thomas Liehr, Marcelo de Bello Cioffi
Scientific Data, vol. 13, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41597-026-08658-2
Abstract The Toco Toucan, Ramphastos toco (Piciformes, Ramphastidae), is an iconic Neotropical bird, yet no high-quality reference genome has previously been available for this lineage. Here, we present the first chromosome-level genome assembly for R. toco , generated using Oxford Nanopore long reads, Hi-C, DNA short-read, and RNA sequencing. The ~1.47 Gb assembly comprises 266 scaffolds, with a contig N50 of 16.95 Mb, and includes 57 chromosome-scale scaffolds representing all 55 autosomes and the Z and W sex chromosomes. Integrated cytogenetic analyses confirmed the chromosome assembly and established the species’ karyotype (2n = 112), providing independent validation of its genome organization. BUSCO analysis recovered 99.5% of expected avian single-copy orthologs, and annotation identified 19,606 genes, including 17,193 protein-coding genes supported by transcriptomic data. Satellite DNA mapping combined with repeat-based prediction identified putative centromeric regions for 52 chromosomes, whereas telomeric repeats were detected in 56 of the 57 assembled chromosomes, supporting the high structural completeness of the assembly. As the first chromosome-level genome for the family Ramphastidae, this resource provides a robust foundation for future studies of avian genome evolution, chromosome biology, and conservation genomics.

item.title: A large dataset of human EEG responses to short naturalistic videos for studying dynamic audio-visual event processing
item.description:
Alessandro T. Gifford, Pablo Oyarzo, Anne W. Zonneveld, Christina Sartzetaki, Iris I. A. Groen, Radoslaw M. Cichy
Scientific Data, vol. 13, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41597-026-08751-6
Abstract Vision neuroscience has experienced a surge in the collection and use of large-scale datasets of brain responses to naturalistic images. However, static images lack the temporal dimension essential for understanding how vision is solved in the brain during dynamic real life settings. To facilitate the study of the neural correlates of dynamic visual event perception, we introduce the EEG Moments Dataset (EMD). EMD consists of 128-channel EEG responses and eye-tracking recordings of 6 human participants viewing 1,102 short naturalistic videos (3-second long; with audio track) while maintaining central fixation. We show that EMD’s EEG responses well encode stimulus-related information, exhibit a temporal correspondence with the video stimuli, and have a rich representational content revealed by brain encoding models based on different feature spaces. Furthermore, complemented by the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD) – an existing large-scale dataset of human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) responses for the same videos – EMD enables spatio-temporally resolved investigations of brain responses to dynamic visual events. We release EMD’s EEG and eye-tracking data in both raw and preprocessed format which is complemented by BMD’s 1,102 video stimuli and rich stimulus metadata. Finally, we provide an interactive code tutorial to familiarize with EMD’s preprocessed data, stimuli, and stimulus metadata.

item.title: A dataset of freshwater bivalve occurrences and associated water quality parameters across 18 European countries from 1989 to 2022
item.description:
Adam M. Ćmiel, Dariusz Halabowski, Anna Małgorzata Lipińska, Agnes Blaise, Teofana Chonova, Anna Cichy, Marcin Czarnoleski, Andreas H. Dobler, et al.
Scientific Data
DOI: 10.1038/s41597-026-08952-z
Abstract Freshwater bivalves are key components of aquatic ecosystems and are widely recognised as bioindicators of environmental conditions. However, understanding of large-scale relationships between bivalve distributions and water quality is constrained by the lack of integrated datasets combining biological and environmental information. Based on the efforts of a network of scientists involved in the COST project “CONFREMU - Conservation of freshwater mussels: a pan-European approach” funded by the European Union, we provide a comprehensive dataset linking freshwater bivalve occurrence records with physicochemical and environmental parameters across European inland waters. The integrated dataset comprises 22,048 records representing 39 species from five families of freshwater bivalves, collected across 18 European countries between 1989 and 2022. This dataset, integrating biological and environmental information compiled from field surveys, published literature, environmental monitoring programmes, publicly available databases and private unpublished data, enables analyses of species–environment relationships across large spatial and temporal scales and supports applications in ecological niche modelling, biodiversity assessment, water quality evaluation and conservation planning.

item.title: Global 30 m Specific Leaf Area Dataset Integrating Large Language Model Imputation and Satellite Remote Sensing
item.description:
Qing Tian, Renxian Zuo, Luwei Feng, Hanliang Gui, Yihao Zhang, Qi Xie, Tianyi Shao, Chen Yang, et al.
Scientific Data
DOI: 10.1038/s41597-026-08954-x
Abstract Leaf functional traits are crucial for understanding plant ecology and ecosystem function. Specific leaf area (SLA)—the ratio of leaf area to dry mass—reflects plant resource acquisition strategies. However, global medium-resolution (30 m) SLA maps remain scarce due to sparse site observations and spatial scale mismatches. Here, we present a modular framework combining large language models (LLMs), machine learning, Landsat optical observations, and environmental variables to generate the first global 30 m SLA dataset with uncertainty estimates. First, LLMs completed missing plant functional type traits in the TRY database (growth form, leaf type, and phenology) with high accuracies (94.70–99.70%), maximizing data utility. Second, a novel landcover-based matching approach aligned site observations with 30 m spatial predictors, overcoming coordinate imprecision. Finally, a Random Forest model on Google Earth Engine integrated spectral, climatic, topographic, and soil layers to map SLA globally. This continuous 30 m SLA dataset addresses key spatial limitations of site observations, while the extensible processing chain can be adapted to other functional traits to support global ecosystem modeling.
